items.title: The UK’s @AISecurityInst (AISI) has published a report on their recent cybersecurity evaluation of Anthropic’s Claude My
items.content:
The UK’s @AISecurityInst (AISI) has published a report on their recent cybersecurity evaluation of Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. The models attempted to complete an assignment in a setup where their normal safeguards were removed and they were deliberately given internet access. AISI reports that the models “engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”.

We’re grateful to AISI for their leadership in the important discussion about how to evaluate increasingly capable AI agents. We’re working closely with them to gather more details of the incident as we conduct our own investigation. Gaining a clear picture of Claude’s understanding of its situation—by examining its reasoning transcripts and running our own analyses—will help us identify the causes of its behavior.

The prompts in the evaluation did not impose any specific restrictions on how the internet should be used. This and the removal of safeguards meant that the models were tested under “deliberately permissive conditions” that are not representative of any of our production models. Note that there was no evidence here of an escape from a secure environment.

AISI’s disclosure of the incident can be found here: https://t.co/cJ3hCBtBU7

1. An agent read your Stripe refunds/
items.content:
23 ways I'd use AI agents to grow my startup to $1M ARR or PMF (my running list):

1. An agent read your Stripe refunds/cancellation reasons, then trigger a different CustomerIO sequence for each, so the person who left over price gets a discount and the person who left over a bug gets a "we fixed it" email.

2. Wire an agent to your PostHog feature flags and have it race two onboarding flows on live signups, auto killing whichever activates fewer people each week. An A/B test that prunes itself!! 

3. Watch your competitor's status page, and the hour they go down, spin up Google Ads targeting "[competitor] alternative" while their users are actively searching. (kind of ruthless, kind of brilliant) 

4. Feed an agent your closed-lost deals, have it draft a personalized reopen email for each, and drop them in your outbox for 1 click send. 

5. Turn your best customer's onboarding into a playbook.md, then run every new signup down that exact path so your best outcome becomes the default.

6. Point an agent at your inbox for positive-sentiment messages and auto-send a Senja review request while the customer is still glowing. And then your G2 page fills itself.

7. Watch for the moment you solve someone's support problem and fire the referral ask right then, while they're relieved and grateful. Timing is everything on referrals.

8. An agent watch your Stripe data for annual customers who never log in, and reach out to re-onboard them, because realistically silent renewers are one bad quarter from canceling so get ahead of it.

9. Catch pricing page bouncers via a PostHog webhook, enrich them with Apollo, and send the objection-handler for their specific industry before they forget you exist.

10. Build an agent that continuously scans for new "best X" and "X vs Y" articles ranking in your category, and auto-drafts a personalized pitch to each writer asking to be added as an option. 

11. Use Apify to scrape everyone who liked your competitor's launch post, waterfall their emails through Apollo, and draft a warm cold email to each. 

12. Build an agent that runs your buyers' top 50 questions through ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity every week, logs which competitors get named and which sources get cited, and Slacks you the moment a competitor starts showing up in an answer where you don't. 

13. Turn your single best-performing post into a landing page, a Meta ad, and a cold email in your voice using a saved style.md, because you already found the message that lands and you're only using it once.

14. Load your founder context into the Ideabrowser MCP once, and every skill your agent runs after that already knows your niche, your customer, and your offer, so nothing starts from scratch.

15. Wire the ideabrowser MCP into your growth agent so every winning headline and pricing test stores back into your project, and each experiment makes the next one smarter.

16. Firecrawl your competitor's docs weekly and have an agent flag every feature they quietly shipped, so you never get blindsided.

17. Watch the changelogs of the platforms you integrate with, so the day Stripe or Shopify ships a new API, you're the first tool built on it and you own that search traffic for months.

18. When a deal stalls for 14 days, have an agent auto-draft the "should I close your file?" breakup email, because that one closes more dead deals than any "just following up" email lol. 

19. Have an agent turn every shipped Linear ticket into the public changelog entry automatically, so your changelog stays current without anyone remembering to update it.

20. Build a Clay enrichment waterfall that scores every inbound lead 1-10 before it hits your inbox, so you only ever open the 8s, 9s, and 10s.

21. Wire an agent to your Resend or Loops data to find the subscribers who open every email but never click, then quietly move them into a harder-CTA sequence, because engaged non-buyers need a different nudge than cold ones.

22. Have an agent read your Stripe metadata to find the customers who upgraded fastest after signup, then trace what all of them did in their first hour, because that's your activation "aha" and you can redesign onboarding to force it.

23. Have an agent watch for the moment a customer's usage doubles month over month, and route them to a human for a "you're growing, let's talk enterprise" call.

These are just a few ideas. Ill keep sharing more here and @startupideaspod if people are into it.

Really into marketing agents right now. These are just some ideas to get your creative juices flowing.

You take a growth task a human used to do, wire an agent into the data and tools that task needs, and let it run on a loop. 

Do that across your business and the agents start making your product better, finding you customers, and pulling you toward PMF or scaling your company if you already have PMF.

Now, go point some agents at your business.

I'm rooting for you.

items.title: When you work on research (particularly on long-term research), you have to accept the fact that corporate management, w
items.content:
When you work on research (particularly on long-term research), you have to accept the fact that corporate management, who is often interested in short-term impact, may think you are wasting your time and company resources. 
But it very much depends what you objectives and your horizon is.

- If your goal is keeping up with the current AI product race, then you might think that long-term bets are a waste.
- If your goal is "AGI" (whatever you mean by that) then your horizon is likely longer and your modus operandi is very different.
- However, If you think "AGI is just around the corner through LLM scaling", then you might think working on world models and other new AI concepts is a waste.
- But if you know that AGI requires a few more conceptual advances (as Demis and I do), you pick a role that maximizes progress towards that goal. That role is necessarily less connected with products, less connected with management, and more connected with research.
- I can't speak for Demis, but in my case, I've always been supportive of high-quality work on LLMs and impressed by the results. My personal interest was to advance towards human-level AI, and I never thought LLMs were the ticket. But I always thought LLMs were incredibly useful as a technology, and eventually as the centerpieces of a family of products.

As a high-level IC (not a manager), I would not have had the influence or power to stifle work on LLM even if I had wanted to (which I had not).

items.content:
comments like this on the aie channel miss the point.

- we are building a community and an industry that is bigger than any one person can hold in their head. your slop is someone's aha moment and vice versa.
- speakers spend quality time coming and presenting their strongest beliefs/entire year's work in 20-180 minutes
- we spend millions on union AV labor and editing to get our speakers a public record that they can then send to customers, employees, and investors
- our speakers are mostly engineers, researchers, academics and founders doing the work; not polished professional talking heads doing the circuit. most talks are prepped <1 week before. most have had ~0 public speaking training. 
- if you want the polished ppl, many other conferences select for people whose main job it is to be great speakers who give great talks
- if you only judge quality by view count, you are guaranteed to be cooked by the algorithm. you will only ever hear about things after they are popular; worse; you consider things good only because they are popular. there are entire industries dedicated to manipulating you. do better.

that said:
- we CAN do a better job in curation. that's on me.
- we CAN do a better job in coaching. also on me.
- we CAN do a better job in production. that's on our team.
- we COULD publish some talks to a secondary channel... I'm just concerned for those speakers as that will start form a smaller base, advice welcome, i am constantly pressured to do this every single year and have said no so far

Jeff Dean just left Google after 27 years to found Discovery Loop to use AI to accelerate science and engineering research.

AI will speed up drug discovery. It does not (yet) speed up making 400,000 doses and trucking them across a complex supply chain.

As I think about the next bottlenecks in AI, I think about the real world. I'm thinking about atoms, not software. Physical, tangible, gets-stuck-in-a-forklift stuff. 

In addition to cleaner and more effective energy sources, we should be looking at companies that have a headstart in manufacturing and making factories faster. Looking at Amazon and large-scale drug makers (Novartis, Pfizer, AZ, GSK, Novo Nordisk, J&J, Merck, Eli Lilly, Roche) obviously. Also at places like Flexe for warehousing, Mytra for simplification of storage, Autostore for warehouse optimization, and Berkshire Grey. This is not investment advice. 

Next decade goes to whoever can produce more (or more effectively) in the physical world.

items.content:
It was running Widrow's supervised Adaline procedure initially, using a pre-determined pseudo-random bit sequence known by the transmitter and receiver modems.
But then it switched to Bob Lucky's self-supervised Adaline procedure in which the weighted sum was self-supervised by its own binary thresholded version.
This allowed the modem to automatically track slowly-changing characteristics of the line.
Bob Lucky and his collaborators at Bell Labs implemented a mixed analog-digital version of this in which the weighted sums were computed in analog, but the weights were coded on 8 bits, implemented by 8 relays.
It was easy to hear whether the procedure had converged by listening to the number of relay clicks per unit time.
Bob Lucky was the Executive Director of Bell Labs Division 113, in which I was hired in 1988 (in the Adaptive Systems Research Department, BL11315).

items.content:
Facebook ads might be one of the easiest places to run an agentic loop.

Here's why it works: running an A/B test on an ad gives you a clear winner.

Build it in 5 parts:

1) Raw material.
- Create a folder.
- Every day, yap at the camera for 30 seconds.
- That is your entire job here.

2) Access.
- Point it at the ad account, not at your description of the ad account.
- It needs the spend and the performance numbers itself.

3) Action.
- Let it cut what's in the folder into variants.
- Different hooks, different angles, a different line of copy.
- On Google search ads it's just copy, which is the easiest thing in the world for an AI to swap.

4) Judgment.
- Every two or three days it looks back at what actually ran.
- Not hourly. The data isn't there yet.

5) Reversal.
- "Cutting the losers, doubling down on the winners."

The catch: budget. Each variant needs enough spend to tell you something, or you're just reading noise.

The other limit is the footage: Fully synthetic ads still lose to ads with a person in them.

Go record the 30 seconds and let the loop test the rest.

items.content:
One of the best applications for agentic loops is SEO.

Here's why it works: the outcome is "black or white."

You moved up this month, you moved down, or you stayed the same.

That's the entire requirement for a loop — a metric that grades the work for you.

Build it in five parts:
1) Access. 
- Connect it to your real data, not your description of your data. 
- Google Search Console has an API. 
- DataForSEO shows you the four pages ranking above yours.

2) Action. 
- Let it audit and fix before it experiments. 
- Meta tags, JSON-LD, a missing sitemap. 
- Quick wins on most sites.

3) Memory. 
- A markdown file where it logs every change it made and why.

4) Judgment. 
- Every two weeks it reopens that file and checks its own work: I rewrote that description — did it rank us higher or lower?

5) Reversal. 
- A change that took you from position 20 to 30 gets undone. 
- Nothing here is set in stone.

Then put it on a routine so it picks up where it left off without you.

The catch: this takes months, not days. 

Months of nothing, then month four, bam bam bam, page one.

So find the number in your business that can't be argued with. 

Build the loop around that one.

Here's the part people get wrong: it's not one loop, it's two.

Bugs and features don't answer to the same number.

Build it in five parts:

1) Access.
- Customer feedback, PostHog, Sentry, your logs.
- Everything a PM would read on a Monday morning.

2) Prioritization.
- It finds the biggest pain points itself, then prototypes features and fixes bugs against them.

3) The bug loop.
- Graded on uptime.
- Objective, boring, no argument about whether it worked.

4) The feature loop.
- Graded on DAU over MAU. Or retention. Or virality. Or NPS.
- One KPI per feature. Let the agent pick it, you approve it.

5) Its own distribution.
- Tools to market itself, so the feedback comes back in without you carrying it.
- Then "go build me a business that helps real estate agents" is an actual instruction.

The catch: "I think this would be risky to do on a real business."

The early experiments are already out there. I assume none of them are working yet.

So pick your two numbers before you pick your tools.

One that grades uptime. One that grades whether anyone came back.

Build. Verify. Repeat.

The catch is the stop condition. Without one it loops forever.

Know what "done" looks like before you start it.

HOW TO BUILD YOUR OWN CUSTOM AGENT SKILLS ON CLAUDE.

it takes less than 10mins to build your own custom skills and you don't need to have any tech skill to do it.

here's how I built one (i've attached a video guide too).

step 1: describe the workflow out loud

type "/skill-creator" and talk. messy is fine, no structure needed. 

it interviews you, pulls the shape out, and writes the file.

I described a graphic style I use for posts. the fonts, the color rules, the render step. that was the entire input.

step 2: let it build the folder

what comes back:
> SKILL.md: the instructions
> reference/: details claude loads only when it needs them
> scripts/: code for the repeatable parts
> assets/: files that end up in the output

only SKILL.md is required. the rest exist so the main file stays short enough to actually get read.

step 3: write the description like you're selling it

the description field is the whole game. it's the only thing claude sees before deciding whether to open your skill at all.

vague description, skill never fires. list the exact phrases you'd type in real life "make me an infographic", "turn this into a graphic". be pushy about it.

step 4: run it once on a real task

this is the step everyone skips.

I made mine render one actual graphic. two things broke immediately. the "hand-drawn" boxes came out as clean rectangles, the wobble setting was too low to see. and the layout left a 300px hole in the canvas.

neither of those showed up while reading the file. both were obvious in one image.

step 5: fix, re-run, look again

that loop is where the skill gets good. not in the writing, in looking at what it produced and fixing what's ugly.

60: Track where GPT makes mistakes and teach your system not to repeat them

64: Ask what improved, what declined, what you avoided and what needs attention

65: Let GPT maintain a live picture of every important project

66: Let it remember exactly where you stopped

67: Let it tell you exactly where to restart

68: Build dashboards only for numbers that change your decisions

69: Use Voice whenever you’re confused instead of letting thoughts sit unresolved

70: Use GPT as the place where ideas enter your life before being routed somewhere else

72: Eventually stop thinking of GPT as something you “use”

73: Talk to it whenever you need to remember, understand, decide, create or act
